top_choice_rationale: P001 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) credits three separable, load-bearing contributions: the tractable time-dependent pricing friction, staggered contracts with the interest-rate rule, and the welfare-based synthesis of interest rates and prices. The work is 25 to 40 years old, has been used in research and central-bank practice, and was extended rather than abandoned after 2008, the zero lower bound and the 2021-23 inflation. The 2022 prize covered banks and crises, not this core. Attribution is the main cost, because Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler are excluded. A citation limited to the pricing friction, the rule and the synthesis, with no claim over the estimated-DSGE tradition, reduces that cost but cannot remove it. I rank P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) second because it has the cleanest attribution and a mechanism distinct from the 2022 prize. Its original contribution is theoretical, with identification coming mostly from later work, and its footprint is narrower. I rank no award last because both proposals reflect mature, original work. I give no weight to the count of colleagues who support P001.
recusal_note: No link to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from the profile. Profile-based connections to disclose: frequent co-authorship and IIES colleagueship with Per Krusell (secretary) and Timo Boppart, and co-authorship with Richard Friberg. Krusell and Boppart support P001 and Friberg supports P002, but none is a candidate. My own research in quantitative macro and climate-economy modelling is adjacent in method to the New Keynesian tradition, so familiarity bias is possible. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
